correctness.rationale: The slice has affine translation space orthogonal to \(\mathbf1\), so every coordinate supporting hyperplane has intrinsic normal length \(\sqrt{(n-1)/n}\). Lower and upper coordinate hyperplanes are facets exactly at the stated strict threshold conditions. When the mass barrier is minimal, all lower facets must occur and summing clearances gives \(\delta\le k/n\); the co-mass case is complementary. When the narrowest-capacity barrier is minimal, both opposite facets of a minimum-capacity coordinate occur and give \(2\delta\le c_{\min}\). Conversely, the three inequalities make the intervals \([\delta,c_i-\delta]\) nonempty with total lower sum at most \(k\) and total upper sum at least \(k\), producing a matching center. The full incenter set is then exactly the shifted actual-facet system.

value.rationale: Slices of rectangular prisms are the central family of the cited paper, generalize hypersimplices, and coincide with polymatroids of Veronese type up to the source equivalence. The theorem gives a complete Euclidean metric invariant for every nontrivial arbitrary-capacity member, not a low-dimensional slice or numerical table. It exposes a sharp three-way phase structure—mass, co-mass, or narrowest coordinate—and completely describes all optimal centers while accounting for the disappearance of coordinate facets. This is a natural metric complement to the established Ehrhart, volume, polymatroid, and Hilbert-function theory.
